1: This briefing comes from Book 16 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, People: Training and Education.
It's written for CIOs and CISOs, workforce and training leads, ISSOs, and help desk leads.
Why do people, not tools, close the gap?
And how do you run the curriculum and measure whether it worked?
The short version: every book before this one changes what someone does.
Tools enforce the new rules, but people run the estate, and a program that trains last pays twice.
Let's start with what tools can't do.
2: Here's the gap in one example.
A Conditional Access policy can require phishing-resistant sign-in for every user.
What it can't do is decide what happens when a caller tells the help desk their security key is lost and they need in right now.
An access review can list everyone with access, but it can't make the owner read the list.
The program's view is that this technology moves risk from configuration to judgment.
There are fewer human decisions left, but each one carries more weight.
And almost every book splits a job into deciding and doing, and hands some decisions to people outside IT, like HR staff and application owners.
Someone who doesn't know the new rule falls back on the old habit, which is exactly what the modernization was meant to remove.
So why not train at the end?
3: Many programs train at the end: build, migrate, then train.
The program's point is that this gets paid for twice.
The first payment comes at cutover.
Users who weren't taught the new sign-in call the help desk.
A help desk that wasn't taught the new verification either turns away real callers or resets accounts without the checks meant to stop impersonation.
Administrators ask for standing roles until things settle, and exceptions granted under pressure tend to stay.
The second payment comes afterward, finding and removing the workarounds and unlearning the habits, which is slower than learning.
And federal rules already put training before the change: before access, and whenever the environment changes significantly.
So training last also puts the agency behind requirements it already has.
4: FISMA is a staffing requirement as much as a course requirement.
The agency head must have enough trained people to comply, and the C I O trains and oversees those with significant security duties.
OPM's rule names five audiences, from every user to IT operations staff, and agencies must code their cyber positions to the NICE Framework, nist's vocabulary of work roles.
But those codes haven't been reliable.
GAO found most agencies had miscoded a share of their IT management positions, so the program treats codes as one roster input, not settled fact.
Just as important is what the rules don't require.
There's no civilian certification mandate, and the Defense Department's certification program doesn't apply to civilian agencies.
Now, what the program actually teaches.
5: The program separates education from training.
Education builds the mental model, for everyone, before anyone touches a tool.
It teaches six ideas in order, because each depends on the one before.
For example: identity is the starting point, one map replaces many inventories, and drift is the feedback signal.
Someone who holds those ideas understands why the help desk now asks for verification, why a role is activated instead of held, and why a screenshot isn't evidence.
Orientation comes in a few forms, including a walkthrough, a self-serve written path, and a short briefing for auditors and assessors.

Then training follows, by role, in four tracks: compliance, for people who evidence controls; implementation, for people who build; vendor training and labs; and end-user training for everyone who signs in.
Let's take the compliance track first.
6: The compliance track is for the people who read evidence rather than build it: ISSOs, compliance staff, assessors and authorizing officials.
It teaches one skill above all, tracing.
Given a control, name the mechanism that closes it, the book that built it, the record it emits, and where that record sits in the authorization package.
Given a record, work back to its control and say whether it's still current.
Orientation covers the essentials, like the Risk Management Framework, who owes which proof, and why Moderate and fed-ramp's Class C are two facts, not one.
Then the modules follow the program's evidence areas, and each teaches a discipline.
For example, a policy screenshot can't show a sign-in was phishing-resistant; only the sign-in record can.
The capstone is a continuous-monitoring narrative for one system.
7: The implementation track teaches the same estate from the engineer's chair, in build modules from D N S and address management through to day-two operations.
The order is a real dependency chain.
You address before you identify, identify before you shape transport, and so on, and day two comes last because it runs what everything else built.
Every module ends the same way: done means it works and its evidence has landed where an assessor can read it.
And every lab teaches three habits.
Keep a way back in, with emergency access accounts created first.
And export the record, not a screenshot.
Certifications are examples, not proof, and they change.
One major Microsoft security exam was just retired and replaced, so the program re-checks its certification list at every gate.
So how does the program certify people?
8: Federal guidance asks for more than completion.
It asks agencies to test knowledge, ideally with practical assessments that mimic the actual work.
So the program certifies only what a person can show, with an artifact someone else could check.
Every capstone is scored on one four-level scale.
In the middle, it names the right books but gets the controls or evidence wrong, or it traces the chain correctly.
At the top, it's assessor-ready: a real, dated result, with an honest statement of what isn't evaluated yet.
An after-action report with no findings scores zero, and so does a training percentage with no per-person records behind it.
Two credentials follow, one for builders and one for assessors, and both expire after a year.
An industry certification can waive a module, but never a capstone.
9: Vendors teach their products, and Book 16 names them as examples, never endorsements.
A vendor course earns a place only if it maps to a book procedure, it's current, the agency can keep the completion record, and the agency knows how the vendor handles learner data.
That record point matters, because exam records tied to a work account vanish when the person leaves.
Lab environments are harder to get than most programs expect.
The free sandboxes are gone, and the developer sandbox isn't offered in any government cloud.
So the program office arranges lab tenants, and before each gate the team rehearses once in the agency's own non-production government tenant.
And every lab follows the same rules, starting with never production, synthetic data only, and tear it down at the end.
10: Every user will sign in differently.
Federal policy requires phishing-resistant sign-in for staff, contractors and partners, and passwords, one-time codes and push approvals don't qualify.
So users learn a piv card, Windows Hello for Business or a passkey, with at least two methods registered.
The course is a handful of short modules, covering sign-in, recovery, devices, where files now live, and reporting.
The last module matters most: what the help desk will and won't ask.
The help desk becomes a target the moment users trust it, and attackers have posed as IT staff to exploit that.
So users learn that the real help desk never asks for a password, a pin or a code, never asks you to approve a prompt for them, and never sends a pass to an address you give on the call.
11: Ask who owns training and three offices answer at once.
Between them, nobody owns whether people can do the new job on the day it changes.
So the program keeps one decider per row.
The sponsor and C I O fund the learning program and decide each wave's readiness plan.
The see-so owns the training policy, the completion threshold, and the exact words users are taught about sign-in and the help desk.
The human capital office owns workforce strategy, position coding, and the facts behind the rosters.
The training lead builds the curriculum and reports the numbers, but never declares a wave ready.
Supervisors own completion, and the help desk manager decides whether the desk is ready.
Contractors can build and deliver it all, but government officials make the decisions.
12: The curriculum runs on the roadmap's calendar, and the planning rule is simple.
No gate is scheduled without its training dates, and no wave without its training window, so a wave that slips moves its training with it.
Each gate carries a training check beside its technical exit.
Early on, the help desk is trained on verification and administrators on just-in-time activation.
Users are trained before their waves.
And by the last gate, no course still teaches an Active Directory procedure.
The help desk goes first: no technician gets a help desk role until their training and verification check are on record.
Before each wave there's a countdown, starting with champions and managers, then the help desk, then users with reminders, and finally the readiness check.
The timings are on the slide.
So how do you know it worked?
13: A completion record says someone finished a course.
Readiness says they can do the job on the day the change arrives.
The program measures four levels, following nist's learning guide: how people reacted, what they learned, how their behavior changed, and what results the gates saw.
The rule is completion for everyone, and competence wherever a mistake is a security event, like help desk technicians and privileged administrators.
For them, completion without a passing assessment doesn't count.
For end users, the most direct measure is sign-in method registration by wave, and it costs nothing to collect.
A wave that isn't ready moves its date, not its threshold.
And the steering committee gets one page at every meeting, in counts, not names, with privileged gaps counted, because each one is a finding.
That brings us to the decisions.
14: Put training in every gate, measured against a roster from HR and identity records, not a headcount, and let a gate pass with a gap only as a named, dated exception.
Train and verify the help desk first, before any new role and before every wave.
Name the owners and keep them apart: the human capital office and the C I O set competencies, the see-so owns the security words, and the training lead reports while others decide.
And certify with artifacts, renewed every year.
The next step needs no procurement.

Build the role roster from HR records and role assignments, name a training lead and an owner for each track, and brief the workforce office, labor relations and the Section 508 program manager before the first gate.
People, not tools, close the gap.
Book 16 has the detail, every claim footnoted.
